Dear Reviewer fCa6, thank you for the reply to the rebuttal.

>The higher-dimensional results are mentioned in the Contributions section. 

Here is the quote from the contributions section highlighting that the main paper focuses on dimension n=2, while appendices discuss higher dimensions n>2.

"Contributions. Problem 1.1 formalizes the necessary conditions for any application-driven ML on real objects. The new invariant Nested Distributed Projection solves Problem 1.1 for all clouds of m unordered points in dimension n = 2...The appendices cover all dimensions n > 2."

>It would significantly strengthen the paper if the authors could provide some experimental results to support these claims.

First, all theoretical results stand on their own because ICML accepts theory. 

Second, all experimental results in section 6 are for 3-dimensional molecules.

>My concern specifically relates to the application of this idea in the proof of Lemma B.9. Could the authors clarify how the base sequence is matched?

Appendix B has Theorem B.9, no Lemma B.9. The proof of Theorem B.9 includes line 1096:

"By Lemma B.3(a) the rigid motion f matches every PR(A; p1, . . . , pn−1) from NDP(A) with PR(B; f(p1), . . . , f(pn−1)). "

So base sequences are matched by a given rigid motion f: any point p_i is matched with its image f(p_i).

In the converse direction, line 1102 explains that a bijection between collections of Point-based Representations gives a match:

"The given bijection NDP(A) → NDP(B) matches PR(A; p1, . . . , pn−1) with an equal PR(B; q1, . . . , qn−1) for some
q1, . . . , qn−1 ∈ B."

>Regarding the graph-based methods mentioned: I don’t believe these methods fundamentally rely on point indices

Science is about proved facts, not beliefs. If you think that all conditions of Problem 1.1 were satisfied by any previous work, could you please provide exact references to the relevant theorems? 

>Could the authors clarify why these methods would require point indices in a meaningful way?

This is the question for the authors of these past papers, not for us. We have proved our theorems. If other authors proved any similar theorems, please give full quotes or exact references (theorem numbers, page numbers etc).

>If the methods presented in the main text are primarily 2D, how were they applied to molecular datasets, which are inherently 3D? 

The main paper said several times that all definitions are generalized to higher dimensions in the appendices.

> I think the presentation can be improved to enhance readability. 

Without examples, this claim can be written about any paper. If anything remains unclear, please provide line numbers.

>clearly highlight the key distinctions of their proposed method, explain how these distinctions change the overall story, and provide a more direct comparison with existing approaches.

All this has been done in sections 1-2. Briefly, the key distinction is a full solution to Problem 1.1: main paper for dimension n=2 and appendices for n>2 with the only exception of Theorem 5.4, which is currently for dimension n=2. 

The direct comparisons with existing (past) invariants are in Tables 2, 5, 7 and Figure 7.

This paper changes the overall story by making obsolete all past machine learning on unordered clouds. Similarly to the side-side-side theorem fully classifying triangles, nobody who knows basic geometry would run machine learning for triangles. It was a big embarrassment that even 4 points in the plane had only a brute-force complete invariant based on all 4!=24 permutations. 

The even bigger and ongoing embarrassment in this discussion is ignoring the significance of the new realizable invariants that established the first efficient definition of a molecular structure. Here is the full quote from the final paragraph in the main paper.

"Most significantly, a molecular structure can now be defined not as a huge collection of vectors under rotations and atom
permutations, see Fig. 1 in (Lang et al., 2024), but as a rigid (class of a) cloud of atomic centers (without chemical elements), which is uniquely determined by an efficient hierarchy of invariants from the fastest (linear-time) SRV to the new complete invariant NDP solving Problem 1.1."

If anything specific remains unclear, please include line numbers and we would be happy to explain.

Thank you to the authors for their additional response. However, I’m afraid my concerns have not been fully addressed.  

1. The higher-dimensional results are mentioned in the Contributions section. It would significantly strengthen the paper if the authors could provide some **experimental** results to support these claims.

2. My concern specifically relates to the application of this idea in the proof of Lemma B.9. Could the authors clarify how the base sequence is matched? This appears to be a crucial step for handling unordered situations. I believe the authors should elaborate more on this aspect.

3. Regarding the graph-based methods mentioned: I don’t believe these methods fundamentally rely on point indices. Typically, such indices are only used for notation. Could the authors clarify why these methods would require point indices in a meaningful way?

4. If the methods presented in the main text are primarily 2D, how were they applied to molecular datasets, which are inherently 3D? This point is unclear and warrants clarification. Additionally, I think the presentation can be improved to enhance readability. It would be helpful for the authors to clearly highlight the key distinctions of their proposed method, explain how these distinctions change the overall story, and provide a more direct comparison with existing approaches.

Dear Reviewer fCa6

>The paper aims to identify a set of invariants for point clouds that can uniquely determine the coordinates of all points up to rigid motions. It also introduces a new measure to evaluate the continuity of the proposed invariants. the desired properties are demonstrated both theoretically and numerically. The evaluation of the claimed properties is acceptable

Thank you for the great summary.

>since the paper asserts that the results hold for any n>=2, they should provide an experiment on a dataset with higher dimensions (n>3).

The main paper considers the 2D case. All higher dimensional results are proved in appendices.

>The proof of Lemma B.5(c) is not clear to me. How can one uniquely choose the linearly independent vectors?

The proof didn't require a unique set of independent vectors. 
 
>What if there is another sequence of linearly independent vectors? Will the resulting point clouds still be the same upto isometry?

The invariance under rigid motion was proved in earlier Lemma B.3(a). For a 2D cloud, only one non-zero point p is needed because any non-zero vector p=(x,y) together with its normal q=(-y,x) defines an orthogonal basis in the plane. However, to get an invariant, all point-based representations PR(A;p) for p in A should be collected in one invariant NDP, see this explanation before Def 3.4.

>The experiment design is reasonable but insufficient to fully justify some of the claims in the paper, such as the method's applicability to any dimension,

The claims in higher dimensions were only in the appendices, because the main paper focused on dimension 2.

>Studying the collection of complete invariants is a well-known, challenging, and important problem. This work mayprovide some valuable insights toward addressing it.

>The related work section could be expanded to discuss existing invariant designs

We can cite the recommended papers as discussed below.

>[1] Is distance matrix enough for geometric deep learning?

The distance matrix is defined for ordered points, not invariant under permutations of points, and was discussed at the beginning of section 2 with references going back to 1935. 

>[2] ComENet: Towards complete and efficient message passing for 3Dmolecular graphs

This paper studies graphs with ordered vertices given by an adjacency matrix, which is not invariant under relabeling of vertices. Problem 1.1 includes the much harder conditions on continuity and realizability.  

>[3] Spherical message passing (SMP) for 3d graph networks

This paper similarly uses angles, which depend on indices of vertices, and include a pair of configurations in Fig. 3(b,c), which are indistinguishable by the SMPs. 

>[4] Theoretically-Principled Sparse, Connected, andRigid Graph Representation of Molecules

This paper again studies representations of graphs with ordered vertices, not invariant under relabeling.

>[5] On the Expressive Power of Sparse Geometric MPNNs

This paper studies generic (not all) geometric graphs. In general position, the classification trivially reduces to the case of ordered vertices as follows: simply order all vertices by the distances to the center of mass. All these distances are distinct for generic (almost all) graphs. Then use the classical distance matrix on ordered vertices. 
 
>as shown in reference [1], it has been established that the Euclidean distance alone is sufficient to determine the coordinates of points up to isometry

Yes, established for ordered points by (Schoenberg, 1935) cited at the beginning of Section 2. 

>[1] also demonstrates that pairwise distances are insufficient to distinguish certain symmetric point clouds. The authors could discuss this limitation and evaluate their method on the challenging examples provided in [1].

[1] presented geometric graphs with edges in Fig.1 and appendix A.1. The underlying clouds and earlier examples depending on 3 free parameters by Pozdnyakov et al are distinguished by the past invariants whose completeness was proved by Widdowson et al (CVPR 2023), see the long discussion of recent advances at the end of section 2. 

Example 4.5 showed the much harder cases: infinitely many 2D clouds (depending on 4 free parameters) in Fig. 2 that have the same pairwise distances but were distinguished even through manual computations in Example C.2.    

>scalability is a crucial concern for this work

Section 6 explained the hierarchical computation over 31 million molecules starting from linear-time invariants, then progressing to stronger invariants and using complete invariants only for rare clouds indistinguishable by simpler invariants, see Tables 2, Fig.7-8.   

>It should also include the algorithm's behavior on synthetic graphs of varying sizes 

Yes, section 5 includes these experiments shown in Fig.5-6.
  
> varying dimensions of coordinates in terms of computation time and robustness to noise

The paper focused on 2D point clouds, because the high dimensional case cannot fit  pages.

"All past attempts by both ML and non-ML in chemistry achieved only 86% on similar size data, see Table 7 summarized in (Vasylenko et al., 2025)"

>[1] Are High-Degree Representations Really Unnecessary

summary.value: This work proposes a representation of unordered point clouds that is invariant under rigid motions and complete (point clouds have the same representation if and only if they are related under a rigid motion). First, the authors provide a detailed specification of the properties required from an invariant point-cloud representation and the corresponding distance defined using such representation. Specifically, they require the representation to be complete, the distance to satisfy the metric axioms and to be Lipschitz continuous, to be able to reconstruct the corresponding point-cloud up to a rigid motion given its representation and to be able to compute both the representation and distance in polynomial time with respect to the dimension of the input. After the definitions of the required properties, they provide a description of the proposed representation (NDP) and distance metric (NBM), along with an extensive theoretical analysis showcasing how they satisfy the different properties. Finally, the authors apply the proposed representation in the task of predicting chemical elements given the geometric structure of a molecule and showcase the advantages of the proposed representation in comparison with previous approaches.

claims_and_evidence.value: The claims of the authors are supported by clear theoretical derivations showcasing how their proposed representation and metric satisfy the properties they aim for.

methods_and_evaluation_criteria.value: The experimental evaluation makes sense since it provides a clear overview of how the desired properties, which were outlined in Section 1, can benefit a specific task on unordered point-clouds.

theoretical_claims.value: The theoretical claims of the authors are backed by proofs that were provided in the supplementary material. The organization of these proofs is quite poor. There is no consistent numbering between the theorems in the main text and the theorems in the supplementary material, and there is no reference in the main text to where the different proofs are located in the supplementary. Additionally, although the authors claim that their results generalize to $n\geq 2$ it seems that Theorem 5.4 is defined and proved only for n=2.

experimental_designs_or_analyses.value: The experimental design is kind of limited to a very specific task involving computational chemistry. While the authors emphasize the large size of the used datasets, both of them contain point clouds with a relatively small number of points. Given the generality of the proposed representation, it would be useful to showcase how it can handle and scale in a more diverse set of tasks and distribution of point clouds.

supplementary_material.value: I reviewed the proofs provided in the supplementary material, I discussed some issues in the Theoretical Claims section.

relation_to_broader_scientific_literatur.value: The key contribution of this work relates to a large field of designing invariant point-cloud and general shape descriptors. Such descriptors are used in a large variety of applications, such as shape classification, point-cloud matching, registration, etc. The authors provide a clear outline of the required properties for such descriptors and showcase how their proposed representation achieves them.

essential_references_not_discussed.value: The literature review is extensive, and I didn't find any significant previous work that has not been discussed.

other_strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths:
- The proposed representation and distance metric are presented rigorously and with a clear description of the motivating factors that affected their designs.
- The generality of the proposed representation allows it to be incorporated into a large variety of point-cloud tasks (although this is not something that the authors specifically showcase in their experiments)

Weaknesses:
- The paper presentation is quite dense, making it harder to read, especially for readers who are less familiar with the topic.
- In the experimental section, the comparison with other ML and non-ML methods is not sufficiently discussed. The authors refer to Table 7 with only a general comment regarding the possible reasons the baselines failed to achieve the same performance as the proposed methods. This makes the comparison less informative for the reader.
- As stated in the comment regarding the theoretical claims, the organization of the supplementary material, especially in the presentation of proofs, is poor, making it quite hard to read.

summary.value: This paper focuses on preserving any output, e.g., class labels or predicted property, when the same object is represented differently, and introduces the so-called complete invariants to satisfy all metric axioms. For validating the proposed method, experiments have been conducted on the "world's largest collections of molecules with 3D coordinates" data. Results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves over 98% accuracy.

claims_and_evidence.value: Seems Yes, the proposed method is claimed that the representation is invariant under rigid transformation. At least from the experiments, the results look like supporting this claim.

methods_and_evaluation_criteria.value: Seems yes. But I think the proposed method can only work with perfect pure synthetic data, e.g., you have a point cloud and mannually rotate it. Under this condition, the proposed method works perfect. It cannot guarantee robustness under noise which is commonly seen in real applications.

experimental_designs_or_analyses.value: The experimental designs are problematic. I really don't like the sentence "The ICML guide for application-driven ML says that 'novel ideas that are simple to apply may be especially valuable', so we start with simpler and much faster invariants below." I think something like this should not appear in a scientific paper. It also sounds like the authors are seeking some excuses for their problematic experimental designs. I think at least the experimental design should include ModelNet shapts (synthetic data, https://modelnet.cs.princeton.edu/) that people usually use to recognize objects under different poses, where some random noise can be mannually added. Moreover, experiments on scene level real-data should be better inlcluded, e.g.,  3DMatch (https://3dmatch.cs.princeton.edu/), to prove efficiency on large scale data as well as robustness on real data. More importantly, this paper has no ablation study on its experimental design, and even no comparisons two existing methods.

supplementary_material.value: Yes, mainly about the code part.

summary.value: This paper introduces a novel approach for machine learning on Euclidean clouds of unordered points, focusing on achieving complete and bi-continuous invariants under rigid motion. The authors propose a new invariant called Nested Distributed Projection (NDP) and a corresponding Nested Bottleneck Metric (NBM). The key idea is to represent a point cloud through a set of Point-based Representations (PRs), which are then combined in a nested fashion to form the complete invariant NDP. The paper claims that NDP and NBM satisfy important theoretical properties: completeness, bi-continuity, realizability, and polynomial time computability. Experimentally, the authors demonstrate the effectiveness of their approach on molecular datasets (QM9, GD), reporting high accuracy in predicting chemical elements using geometric features derived from their invariants.

claims_and_evidence.value: The central claim of the paper is that the proposed NDP and NBM are complete and bi-continuous invariants for rigid Euclidean point clouds, addressing limitations of previous methods. While the paper provides theoretical constructions and arguments for completeness and bi-continuity, the experimental evidence supporting the practical advantage of these properties in downstream ML tasks is not convincingly demonstrated. The claim of "over 98% accuracy" in predicting chemical elements is presented without a clear baseline comparison to other existing methods for similar tasks or datasets. It is unclear if this accuracy is significantly better or even comparable to simpler, less computationally intensive approaches. The paper lacks a comparative evaluation against relevant baselines to convincingly show the benefits of the proposed complete and bi-continuous invariants in practice.

methods_and_evaluation_criteria.value: The paper proposes the Nested Distributed Projection (NDP) as a complete invariant and the Nested Bottleneck Metric (NBM) for comparing these invariants. The method involves constructing Point-based Representations (PRs) using orthogonal vectors and scalar products, and then recursively nesting these PRs to form the NDP. The evaluation criteria primarily consist of demonstrating high accuracy (>98%) on chemical element prediction tasks using QM9 and GD datasets. However, the evaluation is limited by the absence of comparative baselines. The chosen evaluation task, while relevant to the motivation (drug discovery), lacks context in terms of how existing point cloud ML methods perform on similar tasks or datasets. The paper would be significantly strengthened by including comparisons to established point cloud representation learning techniques or molecular property prediction methods. It's unclear why standard benchmarks and evaluation protocols from point cloud analysis or molecular property prediction are not adopted.

theoretical_claims.value: The paper makes several theoretical claims, including the completeness of NDP (Theorem 3.5), the realizability of abstract PR (Theorem 3.3), and the Lipschitz continuity of NBM (Theorem 5.1). While I have not performed a detailed verification of all proofs within the time constraints of this review, the paper outlines the theoretical framework and refers to appendices for detailed proofs (Appendices B, D, E). The theorems themselves appear plausible given the constructions described, and the references to established results (e.g., Dekster & Wilker, Hopcroft & Karp) lend credibility. However, a full assessment of the theoretical contributions would require a thorough examination of the appendices.

experimental_designs_or_analyses.value: The experimental design is centered around evaluating the proposed NDP and NBM on chemical element prediction using QM9 and GD datasets. The analysis involves training a shallow neural network (4-layer) using features derived from the Pointwise Distance Distribution (PDD), which is related to the proposed invariants. The reported accuracy of over 98% is presented as a positive result. However, the soundness and validity of the experimental design are questionable due to the lack of any baseline comparison. It is impossible to assess the significance of the reported accuracy without knowing how simpler methods or adapted existing approaches would perform on the same task and datasets. The experimental analysis would be considerably strengthened by including relevant baseline models and metrics commonly used in point cloud classification or molecular property prediction tasks. The current design only demonstrates the performance of the proposed method in isolation, not its relative effectiveness.

supplementary_material.value:
- Appendices A, B, C, D, E providing extra details, proofs, and parametrization discussions.
- Python/C++ code for computing invariants and metrics.
- Tables with coordinates of colorful maps of QM9 and distances.

relation_to_broader_scientific_literatur.value: The paper relates to the broader scientific literature on invariant feature learning for machine learning, particularly in the context of point cloud processing and molecular representation. The authors cite works from Kendall's shape theory, point cloud registration, and geometric deep learning, including neural networks designed for equivariance. The paper builds upon the existing literature by addressing the specific challenge of creating complete and bi-continuous invariants for unordered point clouds under rigid motion, a problem relevant to various fields dealing with 3D data, including molecular modeling and computer vision. The connection to the "Can we hear the shape of a drum?" problem highlights the theoretical depth and long-standing nature of the questions being addressed.

essential_references_not_discussed.value:
While the paper cites relevant literature on invariant theory and point cloud processing, it misses discussing and comparing against established baseline methods for point cloud representation learning and molecular property prediction. For instance, in the context of molecular datasets and point cloud analysis, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), particularly those designed for geometric data, such as a high-degree version of EGNN (HEGNN) [1] or similar models, are highly relevant baselines. These models are commonly used for molecular property prediction and could be adapted or compared against the proposed invariant-based approach. Including a discussion and experimental comparison to such baseline methods would provide essential context for understanding the contributions of the paper.

[1] Cen, Jiacheng, Anyi, Li, Ning, Lin, Yuxiang, Ren, Zihe, Wang, Wenbing, Huang. "Are High-Degree Representations Really Unnecessary in Equivariant Graph Neural Networks?." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems. Curran Associates, Inc., 2024.

other_strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
### Strengths:
- The paper's main strength lies in its theoretical contribution: the formalization of the problem, the proposed NDP and NBM invariants, and the theoretical claims of completeness, bi-continuity, and polynomial time computability are significant and address a challenging problem in representation learning.
- The concept of realizability and the analogy to geographic coordinates (latitude and longitude) for representing cloud spaces is original and insightful, providing a clear motivation and interpretation for the proposed invariants.
- The theoretical sections (sections 3, 4, 5) are generally well-written and clearly explain the constructions and properties of the proposed invariants.

### Weaknesses:

- The most significant weakness is the lack of comparative experimental evaluation. The absence of baselines makes it impossible to assess the practical significance and advantages of the proposed method over existing approaches. The reported accuracy alone is insufficient to demonstrate the value of complete and bi-continuous invariants in real-world ML tasks.
-  While theoretical completeness and bi-continuity are desirable, the paper does not clearly justify the necessity of such complex invariants in practice, especially without comparing against simpler, potentially incomplete but practically effective methods.
- The experimental section, while reporting high accuracy, does not clearly demonstrate the practical benefits of the proposed method in terms of improved performance compared to existing solutions for molecular property prediction or other relevant tasks.

other_comments_or_suggestions.value:
- The mention of 82GB RAM usage for experiments is slightly confusing. It would be helpful to clarify the system configuration and memory requirements, or if this was a typo and meant to be 80GB. (Minor point, not critical).
- While the supplementary material mentions code availability, ensuring the code is well-documented and easy to use would significantly enhance the paper's impact and reproducibility. Providing links to the code repository in the main paper would be beneficial.
- Adding more details about the implementation of NDP and NBM, including any optimizations or practical considerations, would be valuable.

questions_for_authors.value:
1. The paper lacks any comparison to baseline methods. Could the authors please include experimental comparisons to relevant baseline methods for point cloud representation learning or molecular property prediction, such as Graph Neural Networks (e.g., HEGNN) or simpler invariant-based features, on the QM9 and GD datasets? A response including such comparisons would significantly strengthen the paper's experimental validation and allow for a better assessment of the proposed method's practical advantag
2. The paper emphasizes the theoretical benefits of complete and bi-continuous invariants. Can the authors elaborate on the practical advantages of these properties in the context of molecular machine learning or other real-world applications? Are there specific scenarios where completeness and bi-continuity are essential for achieving better performance or generalizability compared to methods with incomplete or discontinuous invariants? A clearer explanation of the practical benefits would help justify the complexity of the proposed approach.

supplementary_material.value: I have tried to read through the supplementary material.

essential_references_not_discussed.value:
The related work section could be expanded to discuss existing invariant designs, such as those presented in the papers listed below. This paper primarily focuses on fully connected point clouds and constructs invariants from all edges. Adding a dedicated section to compare the proposed method with the approaches in these references (e.g. the pros and cons) would significantly enhance the clarity and contribution of the work.
In particular, the authors should specifically address the similarities and potential limitations in comparison to [1].

[1] Li, Zian, et al. "Is distance matrix enough for geometric deep learning?." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 36 (2024).

[2] Wang, L., Liu, Y., Lin, Y., Liu, H., & Ji, S. (2022). ComENet: Towards complete and efficient message passing for 3D molecular graphs. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, 35, 650-664.

[3] Liu, Y., Wang, L., Liu, M., Zhang, X., Oztekin, B., & Ji, S. (2021). Spherical message passing for 3d graph networks. arXiv preprint arXiv:2102.05013.

[4] Wang, S. H., Huang, Y., Baker, J. M., Sun, Y. E., Tang, Q., & Wang, B. A Theoretically-Principled Sparse, Connected, and Rigid Graph Representation of Molecules. In The Thirteenth International Conference on Learning Representations.

[5] Sverdlov, Y., & Dym, N. (2024). On the Expressive Power of Sparse Geometric MPNNs. arXiv preprint arXiv:2407.02025.

other_strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
There are a few weaknesses that I found in the current method:

- **First**, as shown in reference [1], it has been established that the Euclidean distance alone is sufficient to determine the coordinates of points up to isometry (a result also known in the literature on equivariant graph neural networks). Additionally, after shifting the center to the origin, the matrix of scalar products and the Euclidean distance matrix become equivalent. This suggests that the proposed collection of invariants may not provide additional information beyond what is captured by the Euclidean distance matrix, potentially limiting the novelty of the approach.  
- **Second**, reference [1] also demonstrates that pairwise distances are insufficient to distinguish certain symmetric point clouds. It would be beneficial if the authors could discuss this limitation and evaluate their method on the challenging examples provided in [1]. The code for these examples is publicly available, and I am happy to share it if needed.  
- **Third**, scalability is a crucial concern for this work, as the method appears to be highly unscalable for large point clouds, which is a known challenge in this area [3, 4, 5]. Graphs often comprise thousands or millions of nodes, and having a polynomial complexity on the nodes may make the approach hard to execute on larger datasets in practice. In fact, prior works have explored using sparse collections of invariants to preserve the desired properties while reducing computation costs. A discussion or benchmark comparison with such methods would strengthen the paper. It should also include the algorithm's behavior on synthetic graphs of varying sizes and varying dimensions of coordinates in terms of computation time and robustness to noise.

title.value: Machine learning on rigid classes of Euclidean clouds of unordered points

TLDR.value: The paper develops machine learning based on complete and continuous invariants driven by chemistry applications.

abstract.value: Most real objects allow infinitely many different representations. Robust machine learning aims to use only invariant features independent of object representations to guarantee that any output (class label or predicted property) is preserved if the same object is represented differently. For Euclidean clouds of unordered points under rigid motion, we introduce complete invariants (with no false negatives, no false positives) and a Lipschitz continuous distance that satisfies all metric axioms and is computable in polynomial time of the number of points. The new realizability property implies that the space of all rigid clouds is efficiently parametrized by vectorial invariants like geographic coordinates. The proposed invariants distinguished all rigid classes of atomic clouds in the world's largest collections of molecules with 3D coordinates and predicted chemical elements by pure geometry with over 98% accuracy.

def process(client, invitation):

    domain = client.get_group(invitation.domain)
    venue_id = domain.id
    submission_venue_id = domain.content['submission_venue_id']['value']
    venue_name = domain.content['title']['value']

    now = openreview.tools.datetime_millis(datetime.datetime.now())
    cdate = invitation.cdate

    if cdate > now:
        ## invitation is in the future, do not process
        print('invitation is not yet active', cdate)
        return

    def post_submission_edit(submission):

        updated_note = openreview.api.Note(
            id=submission.id
        )

        if invitation.edit['note']['readers'] == ['everyone'] and submission.odate is None:
            updated_note.odate = now
            updated_note.content = {
                '_bibtex': {
                    'value': openreview.tools.generate_bibtex(
                        note=submission,
                        venue_fullname=venue_name,
                        year=str(datetime.datetime.now().year),
                        url_forum=submission.forum,
                        paper_status='under review',
                        anonymous='readers' in submission.content['authors'] or 'readers' in invitation.edit.get('note', {}).get('content', {}).get('authors', {})
                    )
                }
            }

        client.post_note_edit(
            invitation=invitation.id,
            note=updated_note,
            signatures=[venue_id]
        )
    
    ## Release the submissions to specified readers if venueid is still submission
    submissions = client.get_all_notes(content= { 'venueid': submission_venue_id })
    print(f'update {len(submissions)} submissions')
    openreview.tools.concurrent_requests(post_submission_edit, submissions, desc='post_submission_edit')
